name: Church of San Giovanni Battista
description:
Welcome to the Church of San Giovanni Battista, Riomaggiore’s most significant religious landmark and the keeper of its historical memory. Built in 1340, this church stands in the upper part of the village, offering an atmosphere of rare serenity away from the lively bustle of the harbor.
Take a moment to admire the façade: although it was renovated in Neogothic style during the 19th century, it still features its most precious original element—the white Carrara marble rose window, a 14th-century stone masterpiece that glows under the Ligurian sun. Step inside and you’ll find an unexpected Baroque elegance, with aisles housing treasures such as the wooden crucifix by Anton Maria Maragliano.
The church is easily reached by walking up the main street (Via Colombo). It is the ideal starting point before continuing your climb to the Riomaggiore Castle, located just a few steps away. Visiting this church means immersing yourself in the authentic soul of the Cinque Terre, amidst art, faith and timeless views.

name: Riomaggiore Beach
description: Dive into the magical atmosphere of Riomaggiore by discovering its hidden gem: a small, sheltered cove tucked away right next to the ferry boarding point. This enchanting pebble beach is a peaceful corner where time seems to stand still, letting you enjoy the sound of the sea while the Riviera sun warms your skin.

name: Riomaggiore Train Station
description:
Riomaggiore got its first train station in 1874, the year the coastal rail line connecting the five villages of Cinque Terre was opened. Renovated in 1959, it is located on the cliffside directly above the water, and has views out over the sea and of the town from the platform.  The are regional and high-speed trains: Those traveling south out of the Cinque Terre toward La Spezia stop on track one and those traveling north into the Cinque Terre toward Genoa stop on track two, which can be reached via an underpass with stairs. The platform continues for a stretch inside the tunnel, so passengers can get on and off the train even if their car has stopped in the tunnel. The station has a bar, public restrooms, and a staffed ticket office.

‼️Don’t forget to validate your paper ticket before boarding .  The machines are inside the station, next to the ticket office.
 
♿️Accessibility: The station is equipped with elevators and ramps, making access to the platforms and exits convenient for travelers with disabilities.

name: Manarola Train Station
description:
Stepping off the train in Manarola means being immediately immersed in a magical atmosphere, where the railway seems wedged between rock walls and the sea. To reach the heart of the village, the only way is through the long pedestrian tunnel: as you walk through, take a moment to observe the mosaics and decorations on the walls that celebrate the lives of local winemakers and the beauty of the landscape. Inside the station, you will find the Park Welcome Center, the ideal reference point for asking about trails, such as the Beccara, or for purchasing the Cinque Terre Card. Thanks to the Card, you can access the station's restrooms for free and use the small buses that circulate within the village. If you arrive with heavy luggage, remember that the station does not have an official storage facility, but you can find convenient private solutions right along the tunnel or on the main street leading down to the sea.
Once you exit the tunnel, you will face a key crossroad for your exploration. If you choose to go right, you will begin the climb toward the upper part of the village, where the Church of San Lorenzo dominates the square and where the steep Beccara Trail begins—the perfect challenge for those who want to reach Riomaggiore on foot. If you continue to the left, the road will lead you gently toward the Marina, the small harbor where colorful boats rest on the cliffs and where the famous panoramic path starts for taking that iconic sunset photo of Manarola. While waiting for your train on the platform, always pay close attention to the yellow line: in this section, long-distance trains often speed through, creating sudden and powerful drafts.

A glimpse into the Station’s Past:
Manarola station is not just a place of transit, but a witness to the resilient history of this village. During World War II, the pedestrian tunnel that today teems with tourists was the safest air-raid shelter for the inhabitants: within those stone-carved walls, fears and hopes were shared during bombings. Before 1874, the year the railway opened, Manarola was a world of its own, accessible only via the grueling steps of the Beccara or by sea. The arrival of the train was met with both wonder and fear, forever changing the fate of the farmers who could finally ship their precious Sciacchetrà wine all over the world. Here’s a final fun fact regarding winter: if you look at the hill above the railway exit, you will see the structures of Mario Andreoli’s illuminated Nativity; the thousands of lights that compose it are connected directly to the electrical lines that power the trains, creating a unique link between modern technology and folk tradition.

name: Vernazza Train station
description:
Getting off the train in Vernazza is a unique thrill. The platforms are narrow and mostly carved directly into the mountainside, with tunnels that suddenly open up to the bright colors of the village. As soon as you exit the station, you find yourself on Via Roma, the main street that leads straight down to the sea, lined with artisan shops and the irresistible scent of fresh focaccia. Inside the station you’ll find the Park Information Office where you can validate your Cinque Terre Card or ask for live updates on the trails toward Corniglia or Monterosso. The station provides restrooms (free with the Card) and, while there is no official railway luggage storage, several private "luggage storage" services are located just steps from the exit, perfect for exploring the village unburdened.
Vernazza is perhaps the village where the railway is most seamlessly integrated into local life. Just a two-minute walk from the tracks, you will find yourself in the famous harbor square, surrounded by iconic pastel houses. If you plan to depart after sunset, be careful on the platform for Track 1 (heading toward La Spezia); it is quite narrow and non-stopping trains create a powerful draft as they rush by. Always stay well behind the yellow line to safely enjoy the sight of the trains emerging from the cliff.

A look at the Station’s past:
Vernazza station stood witness to one of the most incredible events in the recent history of the Cinque Terre: the 2011 flood. On that devastating day, a river of mud and debris swept through the village filling the main street up to the level of the railway underpass. The station then became a symbol of rebirth: it was through the cleared tracks that the first aid and volunteers (the so-called "mud angels") arrived to help residents rebuild. Another curious anecdote dates back to the 19th-century construction: engineers were stunned by the hardness of Vernazza’s rock, requiring massive amounts of dynamite that shook the fishermen's houses for months. Today, that same rock shelters the station offering travelers one of the most dramatic entrances in all of Italy.

name: Marina (harbour)
description: Dive into the magical atmosphere of Riomaggiore by discovering its hidden gem: a small, sheltered cove tucked away right next to the ferry boarding point. This enchanting pebble beach is a peaceful corner where time seems to stand still, letting you be lulled by the sound of the sea and warmed by the Riviera sun.

name: Doria Castle, Vernazza
description:
The entrance fee is €2.00.
Doria Castle with its iconic cylindrical tower has watched over the village of Vernazza for nearly a thousand years. It was vuole in the 11th century, this fortress was a strategic military outpost used by the Republic of Genoa to spot and fend off Saracen pirate raids. Perched 70 meters above the sea on a jagged cliff, it stood as an impregnable sentinel in the heart of the Cinque Terre.
Visiting the Castle today means reaching the ultimate viewpoint of the village. After a steep climb starting from the harbor square you emerge onto a terrace suspended between the sky and the sea where you enjoy a 360-degree view of all of Vernazza, the Church of Santa Margherita and the coastline stretching toward Monterosso. It is the perfect spot to capture the iconic village photo from above and lose yourself in the infinite horizon.
During World War II the tower was used as an anti-aircraft station proving its enduring strategic importance. Despite centuries of storms and battles the tower remains remarkably intact standing as a symbol of Vernazza’s pride and resilience against the challenges of history and nature.

name: San Pietro Church
description:
Located in the upper part of the village, the Church of San Pietro is one of the most fascinating examples of Ligurian Gothic architecture in the region. Built in 1334 on the ruins of an ancient 11th-century building, the church greets you with a facade of local sandstone that glows like gold at sunset. The highlight of the exterior is the magnificent white Carrara marble rose window: a masterpiece of perforated stone so delicate it looks like lace, contrasting beautifully with the sturdy medieval walls.
Stepping inside, the atmosphere shifts: the interior is sober and elegant, with Baroque influences blending seamlessly with the original Gothic lines. Be sure to look down at the 12th-century baptismal font and look up at the frescoed vaults. A fascinating detail for visitors is its location: the church was built right on the ridge of the hill, and its courtyard serves as a natural terrace. From here, the silence of the village and the view stretching toward the valley offer a different, more spiritual perspective of the Cinque Terre, away from the typical seaside hustle.

name: Church of San Lorenzo
description:
Standing proudly in the upper district of Manarola, the 14th-century Church of San Lorenzo is a tribute to ancient Ligurian craftsmanship. Its local stone facade hides a treasure: a 1375 white marble rose window, often cited as one of the finest in the region. Stepping inside, you leave the coastal buzz behind for a serene Gothic interior, where centuries-old altarpieces reflect the deep faith of the village’s farming ancestors.
Fun Fact: The church square has always been the true social heart of Manarola. From this vantage point, you can overlook the colorful rooftops and the vertical vineyards above. The detached bell tower reveals the village’s turbulent history: its sturdy design is no accident, as it originally served as a watchtower to spot invading sails. If you visit in December, this place is the "front row seat" to witness the lighting of the world’s largest Nativity scene, which turns the facing hill into a constellation of thousands of lights.

name: Il Gigante (Neptune Statue)
description:
At the far end of Fegina beach, perched on a rocky waves-defying outcrop , stands the imposing statue of The Giant (Il Gigante). This colossal 14-meter-tall figure, made of reinforced concrete and iron, represents Neptune, the god of the sea. Originally, he was depicted holding a massive seashell on his shoulders, which served as a panoramic terrace for the nearby Villa Pastine.
Created in 1910 by sculptor Arrigo Minerbi and architect Francesco Levacher, the statue became the ultimate symbol of Monterosso. Although it was damaged during World War II bombings and further scarred by the great sea storm of 1966—which caused the loss of its arms and the original shell—the Giant remains a proud and powerful figure. Today, it stands as an ancient guardian watching over the horizon and is one of the most photographed landmarks in the Cinque Terre, especially at sunset when its silhouette is framed by the golden sky.

name: Corniglia Train Station
description:
Arriving at Corniglia station is a one-of-a-kind experience. Unlike the other villages, the railway here feels suspended over the water, separated from the town by a massive cliffside. As you step off the train, you’ll find yourself on a panoramic platform where the deep blue of the sea dominates the skyline. Inside the station, the Park Information Point is available for trail maps or to purchase the Cinque Terre Card. This card is especially valuable here, as it allows you to use the shuttle bus connecting the station to the village center for free, saving you a strenuous uphill walk in the heat. If you choose to explore on foot, remember that restrooms are free with the Card, while luggage storage can be found through small private services as you head toward the village.
To reach the heart of Corniglia, you have two choices: the first is the famous Lardarina, a brick staircase consisting of 377 steps across 33 flights. It’s a challenging but unforgettable climb that offers spectacular views as you get to the Church of San Pietro. The second, more comfortable option is the paved road used by the Park buses, which starts right outside the station. Once you reach the top, you’ll realize the effort was worth it—Corniglia is the only village not directly on the water, offering a quiet, bird's-eye perspective of the entire coastline. While waiting for your return train, always stay behind the yellow line, as non-stopping trains speed through this exposed stretch with incredible force.

A glimpse into the past:
Corniglia station hides a story of isolation and ingenuity. Before the railway was completed, the village was nearly inaccessible; farmers had to carry heavy loads of grapes and wine on their shoulders along treacherous paths. It is said that when work began to expand the railway in the 1960s, the station became such a complex construction site that many workers decided to settle here, becoming part of the local community. Another local legend involves "Guvano Beach": right near the station lies an old, abandoned railway tunnel (often closed today) that once led to one of Italy’s most isolated and famous beaches—a hidden paradise beloved by the hippie community in the 1970s. Even though the tunnel is now a relic of the past, the wild and free spirit of this station, nestled between the cliffs and the waves, remains unchanged.

name: Monterosso Train station
description:
Monterosso is the only station in the Cinque Terre that welcomes you with an open square directly overlooking the Fegina seafront. Unlike the other villages, the spaces here are broad and bright. As soon as you step off the platform, you are greeted by a breathtaking view of the famous "Giant Statue" beach. Inside the station, you will find the Park Info Point, where you can buy the Cinque Terre Card or ask for details about the SVA trail connecting to Vernazza. The station features restrooms (free with the Card) and, most importantly for travelers, hosts an official luggage storage service right inside the building— it’s perfect if you want to spend a final day at the beach before heading home.
Upon exiting, two distinct sides of the village await: turning right takes you along the modern Fegina promenade, ideal for those seeking well-equipped beach clubs. If you head left, a beautiful walk through a short pedestrian tunnel leads you into the heart of the Old Town (Borgo Antico), with its narrow alleys and traditional restaurants. As the largest station in the area, many long-distance trains (Intercity and Frecce) stop here, making it the most convenient departure point for those traveling back toward Milan, Genoa or Rome.

History of the Station:
Monterosso station is deeply tied to the village's transformation from a humble fishing hamlet to an elite tourist destination. It is said that when the railway arrived in the 19th century, the locals were the first to grasp the potential of tourism…turning the areas around the tracks into lemon groves and elegant hotels. A curious anecdote concerns the tunnel, connecting the new part of town to the Old Town: before its construction, the two neighborhoods were separated by the San Cristoforo promontory and only communicated via steep stairs or by boat. The railway literally "opened" the mountain, forever changing the face of the village. Also, during heavy storms, waves sometimes crash against the barriers right below the tracks, giving waiting passengers a spectacular display of the sea’s raw power.

name: Ferry riomaggiore
description: The ferry terminal is located at the harbor of Riomaggiore, accessible by following the pathway all way down from the centre and taking the stairs on the left .

name: Monterosso Old Town Tower
description:
It all began around the 9th century. During this time, people living in the inland hills decided to move down toward the coast. Why? The fall of the Roman Empire had made maritime areas dangerous for centuries, but as stable settlements began to form, the Buranco Valley became the beating heart of what we now call "Monterosso Vecchia" (the Old Town).
The name itself is said to derive from the hair color of the noble family that once ruled the area, the Lords of Monterosso, who reportedly had strikingly red hair (Monte-rosso meaning "Red Mountain").

A Fortified Village:
In the Middle Ages, living by the sea meant living in fear of Saracen pirates. This is why the old town is a maze of narrow, winding alleys (called carruggi), designed to confuse invaders and make it easier to defend the town from above.
The symbol of this resistance is the Fieschi Castle, whose ruins still dominate the San Cristoforo promontory. At one time, Monterosso was protected by no fewer than 13 watchtowers. Today, only three remain, including the majestic Aurora Tower and the church bell tower, which originally served as a defensive lookout.

Spiritual Soul and Gothic Beauty:
The heart of the historic center is the Church of San Giovanni Battista (13th century). Looking at its black and white striped facade—typical of the Ligurian Gothic style—you can see the wealth the village achieved through maritime trade and agriculture (especially its famous white wine and lemons, later celebrated by the Nobel Prize-winning poet Eugenio Montale).

Monterosso Today:
Despite the devastation faced over the centuries—including the severe flood of 2011—Old Monterosso has managed to preserve its authentic soul. It is a place where the stone walls tell stories of fishermen, heroic farmers who terraced the steep hills  and a community that  never stopped looking towards the horizon.

name: Monterosso Old Town Beach
description:
The Ancient Fisherman's Beach: Before the construction of the modern pier, this was the very beach where fishermen moored their "gozzi" (traditional wooden boats) and spread their nets to dry in the sun. Today, while it is partially equipped with beach clubs (typically open from May to September), it still preserves a small area of free public beach.

Local Traditions: Every year on June 24th, during the feast of the patron saint San Giovanni Battista, the beach takes center stage with the traditional bonfire known as "Battiston." It is a deeply felt community event that lights up the night.

Natural Features: The beach is composed of a mix of sand and pebbles. Thanks to its proximity to the small harbor and the protection offered by the promontory, the waters are generally calm and crystal clear—perfect for a relaxing break after exploring the narrow carruggi (alleys) of the old town.

Starting Point for Exploration: This beach marks the beginning of the famous Sentiero Azzurro (Blue Trail) that leads to Vernazza, offering one of the most breathtaking scenic hikes in the world.

name: Church of San Giovanni Battista Monterosso
description:
As you wander through the narrow alleys of the historic center, you will be captivated by the majestic facade of the Church of San Giovanni Battista, the primary religious landmark of Monterosso. Built between 1244 and 1307, this church stands as one of the purest and most fascinating examples of the Ligurian Gothic style.

A Lace of Marble:
What strikes you at first glance is the iconic pattern of horizontal stripes in white marble and dark green serpentine stone giving the structure a timeless elegance. In the center of the facade shines a true masterpiece: an intricately carved white marble rose window, as delicate as lace, which seems to glow when caught by the sunlight.

From Watchtower to Bell Tower:
If you look at the bell tower you will notice its sturdy and stern appearance, crowned with battlements. This is because the tower was not originally built for religious purposes; it began as a medieval watchtower. In an era marked by Saracen pirate raids, this structure served to protect the village…it was only raised and adapted to house the church bells.

The Interior: Between Art and Symbolism.
Upon entering, the atmosphere shifts: the space is divided into three aisles which, curiously, widen toward the altar to create an illusion of greater depth. Inside, you can admire the precious baptismal font from 1360 and several exquisite paintings from the Genoese school.

A Secret of Light:
The bond between the church and the village is renewed every year on June 24th, the feast of the patron saint San Giovanni. On this day at dawn, the sun aligns perfectly with the church windows, flooding the interior with a magical light that marks the beginning of the traditional town celebrations.

name: Manarola Scenic Viewpoint
description:
To reach this spot, simply follow the coastal path that starts from Manarola harbor and winds along the cliffside to the north (towards Corniglia). After a short walk along Punta Bonfiglio, you will be standing directly in front of the most colorful facade of the village.

The Magical Moment at Sunset…
While it is stunning at any time of day, the real magic happens at sunset. As the sun dips below the skyline, the pastel houses light up with golden and orange hues and the village lights begin to twinkle like a small nativity scene over the water.

name: Church of Santa Margherita
description:
Built in 1318, this church is unique because its foundations rest directly on the cliffs of the harbor. In Genoese Romanesque style, it is easily recognized by its 40-meter octagonal bell tower overlooking the square. Inside, the atmosphere is dark and mystical, with black stone columns and narrow windows that let in the shimmering light from the waves.

The Legend: It is said that a chest containing the Saint's relics ended up on the beach. Locals tried to move them to a higher location, but a storm magically returned them to the shore. They realized the Saint wanted her church built right there next to the water. Having survived centuries of storms and the 2011 flood, it remains the ultimate symbol of Vernazza’s resilience.

name: Riomaggiore Castle
description:
Climbing towards the top of the village we reach the majestic Riomaggiore Castle, also known as Castellazzo Castle. Originally built in 1260 by the Turcotti Marquises and later completed by the Republic of Genoa, this fortress has dominated the town for over seven centuries. Once a defensive bulwark against maritime raids, its imposing walls and two iconic circular towers house a space dedicated to culture and events today.
Stepping through its gates you’ll be sent back in time…but the real show awaits on its panoramic terrace: from here, you will enjoy one of the most spectacular and dizzying views in all of the Cinque Terre, with your gaze sweeping from the endless sea to the colorful rooftops of the village below. It is the perfect spot for those seeking an unforgettable photograph or simply a moment of contemplation at sunset.
The castle is easily reached with a short uphill walk from the Church of San Giovanni Battista. A must-visit for anyone wishing to discover the noblest and most ancient side of Riomaggiore.

name: Via Dell’Amore
description:
It’s a 900-meter path nestled into the rock of the cliff overlooking the sea, connecting Riomaggiore and Manarola.

This beautiful trail has been closed for 12 years because of a big landslide but  today  it represents one of the main treasures of the UNESCO World Heritage.

Via dell’Amore is a symbol of beauty and romance also thanks  to Gino Covilli’s Five Installations. They make it one of the most evocative open-air museums in the world.

name: Bastion, Manarola
description:
This Castle was built around the XIII century to protect the village from Saracen/ Pirate Raids.
Its remains are now partially incorporated into the modern building that clings to the coast looking over the sea.

name: Punta Bonfiglio, Manarola
description:
It’s the best place for admiring a gorgeous view of the coastline and taking beautiful pictures of Manarola, all while keeping away from the crowds. 

This spot is located on a north sided ridge of the Manarola bay and it’s a 3 minute walk from the harbor, next to the cemetery. There are green areas for sitting and resting with the inclusion of Flowering Trees and picnic tables. You will also find a Statue  of a Girl holding a bunch of grapes.

name: Bell Tower, Manarola
description: This Bell Tower is part of the San Lorenzo Church, representing a 14th-century structure that once served as a defensive lookout against Saracens raids. It stands separately from the Church, offering a panoramic view of the village and the Ligurian Sea. The tower houses a clock and four bells, adding to its historical significance.

name: Innocenzo IV Square, Manarola
description:
You can reach this small Square by walking for about 10 minutes from the waterfront and going uphill by Discovolo Street.
Here you will find S.Lorenzo Church with the amazing Bell Tower that was once used as a defensive lookout. If you're geared up for a steep walk, a path that leads through vineyards  can be followed to reach the top of the mountain, starting from Via Rollandi.

name: Harbour, Manarola
description:
This is the real heart of Manarola…
Fishermen still moor their colorful boats among the rocks creating a vibrant contrast against the pastel houses stacked vertically on the cliff. The Harbour is one of the best spots for photos of the Village, especially during sunset .
You can easily reach Punta Bonfiglio to enjoy a full wonderful view of the whole Town from here.

name: Dario Capellini Square, Manarola
description: This will be the first Square you’ll see in Manarola when arriving by train after walking through the pedestrian tunnel.  Its most notable feature is a large, central circular stone Mosaic with images of local seabirds and fishes. The Square is relatively new, representing a good space for kids and a nice spot for visitors who want to take a little sneak peek of the harbor.

name: Largo Taragio Square, Corniglia
description:
This is the Main Square of the Village, with two particular points of interests:
The World War I Memorial to the Fallen and an 18th century Oratory, dedicated  to St. Catherine of Alexandria.
The Oratory  is a modest building with a simple interior. There’s no entry fee and if you go up the stairs located on the side, you’ll find a terraced area where you can enjoy the amazing view around the back. Here you will be able to spot some restaurants or bars…It’s a pretty place altough very small, with some nice shaded  spots and seats.

name: Madonna Delle Grazie Sanctuary, Corniglia
description:
Also Known with the name of San Bernardino alla Foce, the Sanctuary is located just above Corniglia, at San Bernardino. Originally dedicated to The Saint, who was here in 1485 while traveling from Siena to Genoa, the building got its current title in 1772.
Legend has it that in the 18th century, the inhabitants of Corniglia went there to restore a painting of the Madonna, finding it completely intact however. The current building is the result of the 19th century renovation of a previous chapel, decorated in 1641 by the painter Prospero Luxardo of Corniglia.

name: San Bernardino Square, Corniglia
description:
The small Village of San Bernardino is located between Corniglia and Vernazza, near the crossroads that lead to the two seaside towns. With its 385 meters above sea level, it sure is an amazing spot thanks to the landscape. 
San Bernardino is primarily known for the Sanctuary of Nostra Signora delle Grazie…

How to Get There:

By Car: Accessible via the SP51 road (40-minutes drive from places near La Spezia)

Parking: free and readily available.

By Bus: Local shuttle busses ran by the Cinque Terre National Park connect Corniglia to San Bernardino a few times a day.

On Foot: You can hike to San Bernardino from Corniglia by using scenic, terraced trekking paths.

name: Volastra
description:
Volastra is Manarola’s hilltop Village, arranged in an amphitheater above a hillock between terraced vineyards and olive trees. 
Its name comes from Latin: "vicus oleaster" which literally means "village of olives”.
You can admire a really stunning view on Manarola and Corniglia from here, while keeping away from the usual crowded spots.

HOW TO GET THERE:

-by Car: You can take the provincial road SP370 from La Spezia. At the beginning follow the road signs to Cinque Terre and then after you pass by Manarola, turn right and take SP51 road to Volastra. The trip takes about 35-50 minutes.

-by Bus:
Take Line 29 from La Spezia (the trip takes about 40 minutes) or from Manarola(The trip from Manarola takes about 10 minutes and the ticket costs 2,50€)

-on foot with trail 506 / Caruggio – Volastra  starting from Manarola  Harbour to Volastra (The distance between the villages is about 3km, which makes it a 2hrs steep climb).

name: Madonna Della Salute Sanctuary, Manarola
description:
The Sanctuary is located in the upper part of the town, dating back to the 12th century. It mixes Romanesque and Gothic styles.  The gabled façade crowned with hanging arches is built in a simple way with ashlars of local stone, on which the portal with an ogival sandstone arch is opened, surmounted by a Gothic mullioned window.
The interior has a single rectangular hall, with a barrel vaulted roof. The Gothic arched apse houses a Baroque altar. 
The venerated image of the Madonna was crowned in 1891, but originally the 15th century triptych with San Lorenzo between the Sant'Antonio Abate and San Bernardino was there…it is now preserved in the Church of Manarola.

name: Guglielmo Marconi Square, Vernazza
description:
This is the vibrant seaside Main Square of Vernazza, located at the bottom of Roma Street. 
Facing directly on the sea, It’s surrounded by cafes, open-air restaurants and colorful Ligurian houses.

name: Guglielmo Marconi Square, Vernazza
description:
This is the vibrant seaside Main Square of Vernazza, located at the bottom of Roma Street. 
Facing directly on the sea, It’s surrounded by cafes, open-air restaurants and colorful Ligurian houses.

name: Roma Street, Vernazza
description: This Street represents the central spine of the entire Village and it commenta the Vernazza train station directly to the waterfront at Piazza Guglielmo Marconi. The street is lined with colorful Ligurian houses, artisan boutiques and  local souvenir shops. There are also bakeries, cafes and restaurants.

name: Nostra Signora Di Reggio Sanctuary, Vernazza
description:
The sanctuary is located in a natural Square 315 meters above the sea level, surrounded by cedars and olm oaks. The area hosts the oldest Ligurian cypress( 800 years old). The Romanesque façade is surmounted  by Baroque decorations, like the Black Madonna with Child who supports the scroll of Sacred Scripture, named the "Africana" according to San Luca’s Legend.
The annexed guesthouse was built in the 19th century and is the seat of a Nun Monastery.
Near the Sanctuary there are several tombstones called "column of weeping". It’s a reference to the Legend that tells us of a Knight from The Malaspina Family….he was buried here during the Crusades.

name: Belforte Tower, Vernazza
description:
This cylindrical Tower is the oldest part of Doria Castle, standing on the rocky spur of the Town and stretching out towards the sea at more than 70 meters in height.
After its Restoration in the 20th century, this is the only part that’s left of the Ancient Castle.

name: The Secret Cave, Vernazza
description:
This Cave is a striking natural rock passage inside the Village.
You can reach it by walking  down Vernazza’s main street towards the Harbor, it’s on the left  before Marconi Square.

Passing through this short tunnel will show You a secluded, rugged pebble beach bordered by cliffs and emerald-green water.

name: Guvano Beach, Vernazza
description: This picturesque Beach located between Corniglia and Vernazza was a known meeting place for Hippies and Nudists back in the 1960s. You can reach it in 15 minutes by passing through an abandoned railway tunnel that starts in the Lardarina staircase. You’ll find a beautiful mix of sand and stones here while enjoying some rest since the Beach isn’t crowded very often.

name: New Town Beach, Monterosso
description:
Fegina is a long sandy beach situated in the new part of the Village. This area is perfect for people who are looking for a traditional beach with sand and umbrellas, but You can also settle for free with your own towel. 
The beach is dominated by a  big scenic rock that often serves as the focal point of Tourist Photography.
Along the promenad You can also find cafes, restaurants and small shops.

name: Fegina Rock, Monterosso
description: This huge rock dominates the long sand beach of Monterosso creating a wonderful scenic view, perfect for taking photos.

name: Aurora Tower, Monterosso
description:
The Tower is located at the foot of the San Cristoforo hill, it ideally separates the old Village from the new part of Monterosso.
On one side there’s the beach of Fegina, with the promenade towards the train station, while on the other we find the beach of the Historic Center.

The Tower was part of a larger defensive system that included several buildings, and it’s been probably built in the 17th century from the Genoeses to defend Monterosso from pirate raids.
Today it hosts a lounge bar and restaurant.

name: WWII  Bunker, Monterosso
description: This small old Bunker was  built during the Second World War and it’s located near The Aurora Tower.

name: San Francesco Statue, Monterosso
description:
This bronze monument was installed in 1962 and it depicts the Saint with a wolf, representing his compassion regarding animals.
The Statue is situated on the San Cristoforo promontory: that’s why it  provides a stunning panoramic view of the sea and the Old Town.

name: San Francesco Church, Monterosso
description:
The building Is located on the hill of San Cristoforo, inside the Capuchin convent .
The Church has a single nave surrounded by wooden altars. Inside we can see a painting depicting the Crucifixion, attributed to Van Dick, a Martyrdom of the Capuchin Saints in the counter-façade of the 18th century. You will also find the penitent San Girolamo del Cambiaso, a Madonna degli Angeli of 1896 by Oldoino Multedo and a painting by Giuseppe Palmieri representing the Immaculate Conception with Saints Fedele and Felice.

name: Mortis And Orationis Oratory, Monterosso
description:
The building is located in the main Town Square, next to the Church of San Giovanni Battista. Also known as the Oratory of Santa Maria di Porto Salvo, it was built in the 17th century using Baroque style.
Inside you’ll find a statue of Sant'Antonio Abate, coming from the now unreachable convent dedicated to the Saint.

name: Punta Mesca, Monterosso
description:
The Punta Mesca is  a charming promontory between Levanto and Monterosso, covered by the typical Mediterranean vegetation.

How to get there:
on foot from Monterosso or Levanto (more details can be found in the "trails” section)

name: Scalinata Lardarina (Corniglia Stairs)
description:
Lardarina is brick staircase consisting of 376 steps that links Corniglia station with the centre of the village.

HOW TO GET THERE: Exit the station building and Follow the flat pedestrian walkway to your right, running alongside the train tracks. Within a 2-minute walk, the path will lead you directly there.

(You can also avoid to take the stars choosing the bus).

name: Sanctuary of Nostra Signora di Montenero
description:
Let the Sanctuary of Nostra Signora charm you with its timeless beauty: it stands guarding over Riomaggiore, offering an infinite gaze across the Cinque Terre coast. If You travel to this location by car from La Spezia, follow the coastal road and take the path that climbs towards this haven of peace.
For those seeking a more authentic experience take path 593v after the harbor: it’s an intense but spectacular ascent that will lead you through breathtaking landscapes…

HOW TO GET THERE :
-On foot: Take the SVA / 593V trail starting from the upper part of the village (Via De Gasperi). The path has stone steps that climbs through the vineyards.Time: Around 40–45 minutes uphill. Sturdy shoes are required.
-By car :Drive uphill from Riomaggiore along the SP370 scenic road (Via Litoranea) towards La Spezia.Parking: Park along the road near the Montenero trail entrance (parking spaces are very limited).Final walk: You cannot reach the sanctuary directly by car. From the road, you must walk uphill on a stone path for about 15–20 minutes.

People with disabilities:
For wheelchair users, the Cinque Terre National Park and CAI offer a special off-road, single-wheel chair called a Joëlette. It allows disabled visitors to be safely carried along the flatter trail from”Colle del Telegrafo” to the sanctuary, but it must be booked in advance through the Park Authority or CAI La Spezia.
